item.title: Next Steps with GameJolt Unreal
item.description:
So, this is something I have been working on and trying to figure out: what is the next step?1

What I mean by that is right now, I really have a wrapper around the Game Jolt API that turns API calls into Unreal-friendly calls2. That works, and it gets the job done, but I don’t think it is quite where I want the plugin to end up.

So I want to lay out some of the plans and ideas I have come up with for the next step—specifically, what I am thinking about for the 1.5 update.

I am still planning this update, so I would also really like to hear what other developers would like to see in future versions.

What I want to do in 1.5

One of the big things I wanted to improve is debugging.

I want richer debug messages and a better way of handling logs, especially when something goes wrong with authentication, sessions, scores, or the data store.

One idea I have been playing with is adding a small debug widget along with editor validation.

The widget might look something like this:

┌──────────────────────────────┐
│       GAME JOLT DEBUG        │
├──────────────────────────────┤
│ User:       ExampleUser      │
│ User ID:    123456           │
│ Auth:       ✓                │
│ Session:    ✓                │
│ Last Ping:  12 sec ago       │
├──────────────────────────────┤
│ [Test Login]                 │
│ [Open Session]               │
│ [Ping]                       │
│ [Close Session]              │
└──────────────────────────────┘

The idea isn’t necessarily that this would ship as part of the player’s game. This would primarily be a development and debugging tool.

I’d also like the plugin to be a little smarter about configuration.

For example, if the Game Jolt Game ID or Private Key hasn’t been configured, Unreal could give you something like:

⚠ Game Jolt API credentials are not configured.

Configure them in Project Settings → Plugins → Game Jolt API.

That is a much better experience than finding out that something doesn’t work several API calls later.

Moving beyond API wrappers

The other major thing I want to work on is moving the plugin away from being just a collection of wrapped API calls.

I want to make it easier to use from C++, while still keeping Blueprint support where it makes sense.

With the direction I expect Unreal development to take in the future, I have been thinking a lot more about how I can make the plugin work well for C++ developers without making the API painful to use.

At the same time, I don’t want to abandon Unreal 4 or Unreal 5 users. A lot of indie developers are still using older versions of Unreal, and Game Jolt itself is an indie-focused platform.

So ideally, I want the plugin to support UE4, UE5, and future Unreal versions while giving developers a clean API regardless of which version they are using.

This is something I have fought with quite a bit, and I think I finally have a better idea of what I want the plugin to look like from the user’s perspective.3

Right now, if you want to log a user in through Blueprint, you would have something like:

Event BeginPlay
  → GJ Login (Username, Token)
      → On Complete (bSuccess = true)
          → GJ Open Session

And in C++:

#include "UGameJoltBlueprintLibrary.h"

void AMyPlayerController::AuthenticatePlayer(
    const FString& Username,
    const FString& UserToken)
{
    FOnAuthUserComplete OnComplete;

    OnComplete.BindLambda(
        [](bool bSuccess,
           const FGameJoltUser& User,
           const FString& ErrorMessage)
        {
            if (bSuccess)
            {
                UE_LOG(
                    LogTemp,
                    Log,
                    TEXT("Authenticated: %s"),
                    *User.username
                );
            }
            else
            {
                UE_LOG(
                    LogTemp,
                    Error,
                    TEXT("Auth failed: %s"),
                    *ErrorMessage
                );
            }
        }
    );

    UGameJoltBlueprintLibrary::Login(
        this,
        Username,
        UserToken,
        OnComplete
    );
}

There is nothing inherently wrong with this. In fact, this was intentional.

When I first started the plugin, I didn’t want the library to hide state from the developer. I felt like the developer should be explicit about what was happening and when it was happening.

But after using the plugin and thinking about how I actually want people to use it, I’ve started to change my mind.

I think there is a point where giving the developer complete control just means making them write the same boilerplate over and over again.

So instead, I want to make the common behavior the default.

Ideally, I’d like the C++ API to look more like this:

#include "UGameJolt.h"

void AMyPlayerController::AuthenticatePlayer(
    const FString& Username,
    const FString& UserToken)
{
    UGameJolt::Login(Username, UserToken);
}

The plugin can handle the callback internally and expose a delegate/event for developers who want to react to the result.

That means the developer doesn’t have to manually manage the callback every time they want to perform a normal login.

If something fails, the plugin should provide an error that the developer can handle if they need to, without forcing that error-handling code into every single call.

The old way would still be supported. That’s an important part of this change—I don’t want to take away control, but rather provide good defaults.

Let the plugin handle the boring stuff

I also want to move more of the session management behind the scenes.

For example, the plugin could have settings like:

  • Automatically open session after login
  • Automatically close session when the game exits
  • Automatically ping session
  • Configure ping interval

All of these would be optional. If you don’t like the automatic behavior, turn it off and build your own session management.

Whether you want to ping every 5, 30, or 60 seconds, you can set it up to fit your workflow.

The goal isn’t to lock developers into one way of doing things. It’s to make the normal case require less work.

I think that is the biggest philosophy change I want to make with 1.5. When I first built the plugin, I wanted the developer to explicitly own the state. Now I think the better approach is:

The plugin should own the state by default, but the developer should always be able to take control of it.

That feels like a much better balance.

Release process

Those are the big changes I currently have planned for 1.5.

There are also some smaller infrastructure changes happening around the project. I am currently moving most of my repositories over to release-please so I can have a more consistent release process, and I will be moving this project over to it as well.

Hopefully, that should make releases a little less manual and make it easier to keep the changelog and versioning consistent.

Implementation Ideas

Now we get to the part I am still trying to figure out. I have three different approaches in mind for how I could actually implement these changes.

1. “Subsystem Lite”

I removed the subsystem from the early versions of the plugin going into 1.0, but I’ve been thinking about bringing it back in a much lighter form.

I don’t want to marry the entire plugin to the subsystem, but I think it could provide a much cleaner interface for what I am trying to accomplish.

Instead of:

Get something
→ Call function
→ Create callback
→ Handle callback

you could have:

Get Game Jolt Subsystem
        ↓
      Login
        ↓
    On Login

The subsystem would initially expose things like:

UGameInstanceSubsystem
└── UGameJoltSubsystem
    ├── Login()
    ├── Logout()
    ├── OpenSession()
    ├── CloseSession()
    ├── SubmitScore()
    ├── FetchScores()
    ├── FetchTrophies()
    ├── SetUserData()
    └── GetUserData()

Which, if we’re being honest, is basically what the plugin already does. The difference is the interface.

This would get rid of the need to pass this around and would give me a cleaner place to manage delegates, state, sessions, authentication, and error handling. And yes, I love lambdas, but I think this would be a better flow for the person actually using the plugin.

2. “Don’t Rework It — Improve the DX/UX”

The second option is much less invasive.

Instead of changing the entire architecture, I could keep the current API and focus on improving the developer experience around it. That would include things like the debug widget and editor validation I mentioned earlier.

Another thing I would like to add is proper result structures. Right now, a lot of operations essentially return:

bool bSuccess;
FString ErrorMessage;

I would rather have something like:

FGameJoltResult
{
    bool bSuccess;
    FString ErrorMessage;
    int32 ErrorCode;
};

That gives the plugin a standardized way to report errors. Instead of having every API call invent its own error handling, the plugin could provide consistent error codes and result structures across the entire API.

Then we could build more useful structures on top of that:

FGameJoltUser
FGameJoltScore
FGameJoltTrophy
FGameJoltData
FGameJoltResult

This wouldn’t fundamentally change how the plugin works—it would just make the existing API cleaner and easier to build on.

3. Something in between

The third option is probably the one I am currently leaning toward.

Instead of completely replacing the existing API or doing nothing more than polishing it, I could introduce a higher-level interface while keeping the current API underneath it.

Something like:

                 Game Jolt Plugin
                       │
          ┌────────────┴────────────┐
          │                         │
    High-Level API             Low-Level API
          │                         │
    GameJoltSubsystem       Blueprint Library
          │                         │
          └────────────┬────────────┘
                       │
                  API Layer
                       │
                  Game Jolt

The high-level API would handle the common cases (authentication state, session state, automatic pings, automatic cleanup, delegates, and error handling). The lower-level API would still exist for developers who want direct control.

That would let the plugin have sane defaults without turning it into a black box, and honestly, that is probably the direction I want the plugin to take.

So, what’s next?

I don’t have all of this figured out yet. That’s kind of the point of this post.

The 1.5 update is still in the planning stage, and I want to use this time to figure out what would actually be useful rather than just adding features because I can.

The big question I keep coming back to is:

How much should the plugin do for you?

I don’t want it to be a thin HTTP wrapper where you have to manage every piece of state yourself. But I also don’t want it to become a giant black box where you have no idea what is happening underneath.

I think there is a good middle ground somewhere between those two. For 1.5, I want to find it.

If you are using the plugin, I’d especially like to hear what would make it easier for your workflow: * Would you prefer a subsystem? * A simpler C++ API? * Better Blueprint nodes? * Better debugging tools? * More Game Jolt API support? * Or something completely different?

Let me know.

Footnotes

  1. One small step for man, one giant leap for mankind. Some would say.↩︎

  2. “Safe” being that it’s running through Unreal-managed code, not because I magically made HTTP requests safe.↩︎

  3. The user being the developer using the plugin, not the end user playing the game.↩︎

item.title: ML-Physics: Teaching a Neural Net to Fake Physics
item.description:
So I don’t talk about this much on here, but I have been quietly building something I think is actually kind of cool — a 2D physics engine where the classical solver trains a neural net to eventually replace the expensive parts of itself. The long-term goal is to get something that can run KSP or Space Engine scale simulations on mid-range hardware. That’s the dream anyway.

Let me explain what I mean, because I feel like this gets misunderstood fast.

What Even Is a Constraint Solver?

A classical rigid body physics engine works by defining constraints — rules that the simulation has to satisfy every frame. Things like “these two boxes cannot overlap” or “this joint has to stay connected.” Every frame, the solver looks at all the violations and applies corrective impulses to the bodies to fix them. The specific method I am using is called a sequential impulse solver, which is what Box2D uses and what Erin Catto has been writing about for years in his GDC papers.1

The cool thing about this approach is it is deterministic. Same inputs, same outputs, every time. That matters a lot for what comes next.

Code 
{
  const w = 640, h = 320;
  const svg = d3.create("svg")
    .attr("viewBox", `0 0 ${w} ${h}`)
    .attr("width", "100%")
    .style("font-family", "system-ui, sans-serif");

  const defs = svg.append("defs");

    g.append("line")
      .attr("x1",x1).attr("y1",y1).attr("x2",x2).attr("y2",y2)
      .attr("stroke","#bbb").attr("stroke-width",1.2)

  arrow(root, 320, 64, 320, 94);
  root.append("text").attr("x",335).attr("y",83)
    .attr("font-size",11).attr("fill","#bbb").text("dt = 1/60s");

  const steps = [
    { y:94,  title:"Integrate forces",      sub:"Semi-implicit Euler, gravity",    ms:"~0.2ms" },
    { y:178, title:"Broadphase",            sub:"AABB overlap, O(n²) for now",     ms:"~0.5ms" },
    { y:262, title:"Narrowphase + resolve", sub:"SAT, sequential impulse solver",  ms:"~2-8ms" },
  ];

  steps.forEach((s, i) => {
    box(root, 200, s.y, 240, 54, teal, s.title, s.sub);
    if (i < steps.length - 1) arrow(root, 320, s.y+54, 320, s.y+84);
    root.append("text").attr("x",60).attr("y",s.y+27)
      .attr("text-anchor","middle").attr("font-size",11).attr("fill","#bbb").text(s.ms);
  });

  root.append("text").attr("x",60).attr("y",42)
    .attr("text-anchor","middle").attr("font-size",11).attr("fill","#bbb")
    .text("budget: 16.6ms");

  root.append("path")
    .attr("d","M440 289 L540 289 L540 42 L400 42")
    .attr("fill","none").attr("stroke","#ccc")
    .attr("stroke-width",1).attr("stroke-dasharray","5 4")
    .attr("marker-end","url(#arr)");

  root.append("text").attr("x",554).attr("y",170)
    .attr("text-anchor","middle").attr("font-size",11).attr("fill","#bbb")
    .attr("transform","rotate(-90 554 170)").text("next frame");

  return svg.node();
}

So Where Does the ML Come In?

Here is the thing — constraint solvers scale badly. The more bodies you have, the more constraints you have, the more work the solver has to do every frame. KSP2 is a great example of this going wrong. Every part of every vessel is running through a full constraint solve every frame, and the game runs like garbage on anything but high end hardware.

The idea I am working with is: similar physical configurations tend to produce similar outcomes. A stack of boxes falling looks basically the same whether it’s these three boxes or those three boxes. A neural net can learn to recognize those patterns and predict what the solver would have done — without actually running the solver.

So the pipeline is basically:

  1. Run the classical solver on a bunch of random scenarios
  2. Record every (state before step, state after step) pair
  3. Train a small neural net to learn that mapping
  4. At runtime, route “boring” or “familiar” physics through the net, and fall back to the real solver for anything complex or novel

The thing that makes this actually viable is that the solver generates its own training data. I don’t need a dataset. I just need to run the engine.2

{
  const n = bodyCount;
  const frames = Array.from({length:25}, (_,i) => (i+1)*10);
  const solverMs = frames.map(b => +(b*b*0.002 + b*0.02).toFixed(1));
  const overBudget = (+(n*n*0.002 + n*0.02).toFixed(1)) > 16.6;

  const iW=w-mL-mR, iH=h-mT-mB;
  const xS = d3.scaleLinear([10,250],[0,iW]);

    .attr("width","100%").style("font-family","system-ui, sans-serif");
  const g = svg.append("g").attr("transform",`translate(${mL},${mT})`);

  yS.ticks(5).forEach(t => {
    g.append("line").attr("x1",0).attr("x2",iW)
      .attr("y1",yS(t)).attr("y2",yS(t))
      .attr("stroke","#e5e5e3").attr("stroke-width",1);
  });

  g.append("line").attr("x1",0).attr("x2",iW)
    .attr("y1",yS(16.6)).attr("y2",yS(16.6))
    .attr("stroke","#e24b4a").attr("stroke-width",1.5)
    .attr("stroke-dasharray","6 4");
  g.append("text").attr("x",iW-4).attr("y",yS(16.6)-5)
    .attr("text-anchor","end").attr("font-size",10).attr("fill","#e24b4a")
    .text("16.6ms budget");

  g.append("path")
    .datum(frames.map((f,i)=>[f,0.8]))
    .attr("fill","rgba(27,175,122,0.08)")
    .attr("d", d3.area().x(d=>xS(d[0])).y0(iH).y1(d=>yS(d[1])));
  g.append("path")
    .datum(frames.map((f,i)=>[f,0.8]))
    .attr("fill","none").attr("stroke","#1baf7a").attr("stroke-width",2)
    .attr("d", d3.line().x(d=>xS(d[0])).y(d=>yS(d[1])));

  g.append("path")
    .datum(frames.map((f,i)=>[f,solverMs[i]]))
    .attr("fill","rgba(42,120,214,0.08)")
    .attr("d", d3.area().x(d=>xS(d[0])).y0(iH).y1(d=>yS(Math.min(d[1],130))));
  g.append("path")
    .datum(frames.map((f,i)=>[f,solverMs[i]]))
    .attr("fill","none").attr("stroke","#2a78d6").attr("stroke-width",2)
    .attr("d", d3.line().x(d=>xS(d[0])).y(d=>yS(Math.min(d[1],130))));

  g.append("line")
    .attr("x1",xS(n)).attr("x2",xS(n)).attr("y1",0).attr("y2",iH)
    .attr("stroke", overBudget ? "#e24b4a" : "#999")
    .attr("stroke-width",1).attr("stroke-dasharray","4 3");
  g.append("circle")
    .attr("cx",xS(n)).attr("cy",yS(Math.min(solverAtN,128)))
    .attr("r",5).attr("fill", overBudget ? "#e24b4a" : "#2a78d6");
  g.append("text")
    .attr("x",xS(n)+6).attr("y",yS(Math.min(solverAtN,125))-6)
    .attr("font-size",10).attr("fill", overBudget ? "#e24b4a" : "#2a78d6")
    .text(`${n} bodies → ${solverAtN}ms${overBudget ? " ⚠ over budget" : ""}`);

  g.append("g").attr("transform",`translate(0,${iH})`)
    .call(d3.axisBottom(xS).ticks(8))
    .selectAll("text").attr("fill","#898781").attr("font-size",10);
  g.append("g")
    .call(d3.axisLeft(yS).ticks(5).tickFormat(d=>d+"ms"))
    .selectAll("text").attr("fill","#898781").attr("font-size",10);

  g.append("text").attr("x",iW/2).attr("y",iH+34)
    .attr("text-anchor","middle").attr("font-size",11).attr("fill","#898781")
    .text("Bodies in scene");
  g.append("text").attr("transform","rotate(-90)")
    .attr("x",-iH/2).attr("y",-42)
    .attr("text-anchor","middle").attr("font-size",11).attr("fill","#898781")
    .text("Frame time (ms)");

  const leg = svg.append("g").attr("transform",`translate(${mL},8)`);
  [["#2a78d6","Classical solver O(n²)"],["#1baf7a","Neural approximator"],["#e24b4a","Frame budget"]].forEach(([c,l],i)=>{
    leg.append("rect").attr("x",i*180).attr("y",0).attr("width",10).attr("height",10).attr("rx",2).attr("fill",c);
    leg.append("text").attr("x",i*180+14).attr("y",9).attr("font-size",10).attr("fill","#666").text(l);
  });

  return svg.node();
}

Where It’s At Right Now

The 2D engine is built in C++ using xmake — broadphase collision detection, SAT narrowphase for circles and boxes, sequential impulse resolution, the whole thing. It runs a multithreaded data generator that spins up one physics world per CPU thread, runs random scenarios, and writes binary files that Python can read for training.

The neural net itself is a small residual MLP — predicts the change in state rather than the absolute state, which keeps the outputs small and makes training way more stable. About 531k parameters, which is nothing. Runs in under a millisecond on any modern GPU.

I am still in early days — first real training run hasn’t finished yet — but the pipeline is working end to end. TensorBoard is logging everything including side-by-side videos of what the solver does vs what the net predicts, so I can actually see where it diverges.3

Why 2D First?

Honestly, 2D is just a proving ground. The goal is 3D, targeting RTX 30x0 as the minimum. But 3D introduces a bunch of problems that 2D doesn’t have — rotation alone gets way more complicated (quaternions are annoying for neural nets, there’s actually a whole paper on this4), and contact geometry becomes dramatically harder.

The 2D engine gives me a working data pipeline I can trust, training infrastructure I know works, and something to write about while the harder stuff is being figured out. Also it’s just easier to debug when you can see everything in a flat 2D view.

What’s Next

Getting the first training run done and looking at rollout stability — that’s the real metric that matters. A 1% position error per frame sounds small until you realize it compounds into garbage after about two seconds of simulation. The question is how many frames the net can run unassisted before it needs a correction from the real solver.

Drag the slider. See how fast it falls apart.

  value: 1.0, step: 0.1, label: "Per-frame error rate (%)"
})

  const FRAMES=300, THRESH=0.5;
  const rate = errorPct/100;
  const fl = Array.from({length:FRAMES},(_,i)=>i);
  const rollout = fl.map(i => Math.min(Math.pow(1+rate,i)-1, 8));

  const w=640,h=260,mL=55,mR=20,mT=24,mB=40;
  const iW=w-mL-mR, iH=h-mT-mB;
  const xS=d3.scaleLinear([0,FRAMES],[0,iW]);
